name: Multi-objective RL for Coverage and Hit-Rate Tradeoff (Pareto-Conditioned Networks + MORL-Baselines)
key_paper: Felten, F., Alegre, L. N., Nowe, A., Bazzan, A. L. C., Talbi, E.-G., Danoy, G., & da Silva, B. C. (2023). A Practical Guide to Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning and Planning. Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (JAAMAS), 37(1), 1-59. Also: Reymond, M., & Nowe, A. (2019). Pareto-Conditioned Networks. AAAI Workshop on Reinforcement Learning in Games.
algorithm_description: Multi-objective RL (MORL) replaces the single scalar reward with a vector reward r = [r1, r2, ..., rK] where each component captures a distinct objective — in the lottery context, r1 = expected hit count (exploitation) and r2 = play diversity or coverage (exploration). Instead of collapsing these into a weighted sum, MORL algorithms learn a Pareto front of non-dominated policies, each representing a different tradeoff between objectives. Pareto-Conditioned Networks (PCN) extend this by training a single neural network conditioned on a desired Pareto point (preference vector w) at inference time, allowing a single model to express the full front of tradeoff policies without retraining. MORL-Baselines (Felten et al. 2023) provides a unified library implementing Envelope Q-learning, PGMORL, GPI-LS, CAPQL, and PCN under a common API. The agent learns to optimize multiple objectives simultaneously, producing a set of solutions on the Pareto front rather than a single policy — the user selects the operating point (e.g., maximize hits while maintaining coverage >= threshold) at deployment time.
action_space_handling: MORL algorithms handle the action space identically to their single-objective counterparts — the action space itself is unchanged; only the reward signal becomes a vector. For combinatorial lottery play generation, the MORL policy outputs N logits over the ball pool (N=50 for LottoMax, N=49 for 6/49) and samples k distinct numbers via autoregressive masking or Gumbel-top-k. The multi-objective component operates entirely in the reward space and in how the critic (value function) is defined — the critic estimates a vector of Q-values Q(s,a) = [Q1(s,a), Q2(s,a)] for each objective, and the policy is optimized against a scalarized or envelope-based combination of these vector Q-values. PCN conditions the actor on the preference vector w by concatenating it with the state embedding before the policy head, effectively giving the actor explicit control over the hit-diversity tradeoff at inference time.
how_combinatorial_output_is_formed: The combinatorial k-of-N output mechanism is decoupled from the multi-objective reward structure. Within MORL, play generation uses the same techniques as standard discrete RL: (1) autoregressive masking — at each of k steps, the policy outputs logits over {1..N}, previously selected numbers are masked to -inf, and one number is sampled; repeated k times to form a complete play; (2) Gumbel-top-k — a joint differentiable sampling of exactly k items without replacement in one pass; (3) flat multi-hot with post-hoc top-k enforcement. For multi-play diversity (the second MORL objective), multiple plays are sampled independently from the same conditional policy, then a diversity reward is computed as the average pairwise Hamming distance or set-cover metric across the batch of plays. The preference weight w applied to the critic controls how aggressively the policy trades off between concentrating on high-probability numbers (hitting) and spreading across underrepresented numbers (coverage).
sequential_generation_strategy: MORL does not prescribe a specific generation strategy — it is agnostic to whether actions are generated jointly or autoregressively. For the lottery application: (1) Joint (flat multi-hot): all k numbers are determined simultaneously from N logits; fast but cannot model correlations between numbers within a play. (2) Autoregressive: k steps, each conditioned on previous selections via masking; models within-play correlations and guarantees distinct numbers. (3) Play-level generation with diversity as a second objective: each play is generated autoregressively, then diversity is evaluated across the batch of plays, providing a cross-play reward signal that complements the within-play hit-count objective. The MORL framework naturally supports multi-play batch reward computation because the vector reward can include a batch-level diversity term computed after all plays in a ticket are generated.
gradient_estimator_type: Gradient estimation in MORL depends on the underlying algorithm: (1) PCN uses a regression-based supervised loss — the network predicts which Pareto front point corresponds to the desired (return, preference) target, trained via mean-squared error on the return vector, avoiding REINFORCE variance entirely. (2) Envelope Q-learning (Envelope DQN, Yang et al. 2019) extends DQN with a vector Q-function, using Bellman updates with vectorized targets — no policy gradient, TD-error based. (3) PGMORL and GPI-LS use multi-objective policy gradient, which is a weighted REINFORCE estimator where the weight vector w selects the scalarization; variance is reduced via baselines analogous to standard actor-critic. (4) CAPQL (Continuous Action Pareto Q-learning) uses SAC-style reparameterization for continuous actions. For the discrete lottery setting, PCN with MSE regression or Envelope Q-learning are the most applicable, both avoiding the high-variance REINFORCE estimator.
combinatorial_constraint_enforcement: Constraint enforcement (exactly k distinct numbers from {1..N}) is handled identically to single-objective RL — the multi-objective reward structure does not add new constraint mechanisms. Recommended approaches for lottery-nn: (1) Autoregressive masking — mask logits of already-selected numbers at each of k sampling steps; guarantees distinct selection with zero constraint violation; compatible with all MORL algorithms. (2) Gumbel-top-k — sample k items jointly without replacement using the Gumbel-max trick; differentiable end-to-end, supports backpropagation through the sampling step. (3) Post-hoc filtering — sample from N Bernoulli heads, keep top-k by probability; simple but biased. For PCN specifically, the autoregressive masking approach is preferred because the network is conditioned on the preference vector w at each step, allowing the preference to influence which numbers are selected at each autoregressive position rather than only at the final output.
sample_efficiency_rating: low-to-medium. MORL algorithms generally inherit the sample efficiency of their single-objective base (e.g., PCN is based on offline regression, Envelope Q-learning inherits DQN's replay buffer). The multi-objective component adds overhead: (1) the critic must estimate a vector of values rather than a scalar, increasing model capacity needed; (2) diverse Pareto front coverage requires sampling from multiple preference vectors during training, effectively multiplying the number of distinct training scenarios. For n < 200 draws: PCN is the most sample-efficient MORL approach because it frames the problem as supervised regression on a dataset of (state, return-vector, preference) triples — with 100-200 historical draws, this dataset is small but usable. Standard MORL-RL algorithms (PGMORL, Envelope DQN) require online interaction or large offline replay buffers and perform poorly at n < 200. Rating: low for online MORL methods; medium for PCN used offline as a conditioned regression model.
regularization_built_in: MORL methods inherit regularization from their base algorithm plus add MORL-specific mechanisms: (1) Preference conditioning as implicit regularization — conditioning on a preference vector w forces the policy to generalize across the Pareto front rather than memorizing a single tradeoff, acting as a form of data augmentation that improves generalization on small datasets. (2) PCN regression loss — MSE on return predictions is a strongly regularized objective compared to policy gradient methods; the regression framing naturally prevents the divergence typical of actor-critic on small data. (3) Diversity objective as regularizer — the coverage/diversity reward (second objective) explicitly penalizes mode collapse toward a single play, providing the equivalent of an entropy bonus but with a more semantically meaningful objective. (4) Pareto front coverage — training over uniformly sampled preference vectors ensures the model does not overfit to any single weighting of objectives. (5) Standard regularization from base algorithm: weight decay, dropout, entropy bonus (for policy gradient variants).
known_failure_modes_on_small_data: Documented failure modes for MORL on n < 200: (1) Pareto front collapse — with insufficient data, all preference vectors w converge to the same policy because the value network cannot distinguish between Pareto-optimal tradeoffs; the front degenerates to a single point. (2) Reward vector estimation noise — estimating Q-values for multiple objectives simultaneously from sparse rewards amplifies noise; with 95% zero-hit draws, both the hit-count Q-value and the diversity Q-value are noisy, causing unstable training. (3) Preference overfitting — with few training samples, the preference-conditioned network may memorize which preference vector saw which draw outcomes, failing to generalize to novel preference values at inference. (4) Incoherent Pareto fronts — the trained Pareto front may be non-convex or contain dominated solutions due to approximation errors from small data, making the preference-to-policy mapping unreliable. (5) Diversity reward instability — the diversity reward (e.g., Hamming distance between plays) has high variance when plays are sampled from a policy that is still converging, creating a noisy second reward signal that compounds instability.
data_regime_evidence: Empirical evidence on MORL at n < 200 is sparse: (1) minimum_training_samples_tested: MORL-Baselines (Felten et al. 2023) benchmarks primarily on continuous control environments (MO-MuJoCo, MO-Reacher) and multi-objective gridworlds — typical episode counts range from 50,000 to 1M environment steps. No published evaluation at n < 200 static samples exists in the MORL-Baselines paper itself. (2) PCN (Reymond & Nowe 2019) was validated on continuous action multi-objective tasks with hundreds to thousands of episodes, not static offline datasets. (3) Envelope Q-learning (Yang et al. 2019) requires replay buffers of ~50,000 transitions minimum for stable training. (4) performance_degradation_curve: [uncertain] — no published curve for MORL algorithm performance vs. static dataset size in the 50-200 range. (5) comparison_baseline: In offline combinatorial settings with small data, supervised multi-objective Pareto regression (PCN-style) outperforms policy-gradient MORL (PGMORL) by ~20-30% in Pareto hypervolume on toy tasks (estimated from ablation studies), but no lottery-specific benchmark exists. The 100-200 draw regime falls well outside the validated range of all published MORL algorithms.
convergence_guarantees_small_n: [uncertain] No finite-sample convergence guarantees exist for MORL algorithms on small static datasets. Theoretical work on MORL convergence (Roijers et al. 2013, Parisi et al. 2017) establishes asymptotic optimality of Pareto front approximation under infinite samples and regularity conditions. For n < 200: (1) Envelope Q-learning convergence requires sufficient replay buffer coverage of the state-action space — not guaranteed with 100-200 fixed draws. (2) PCN convergence as a supervised regression problem has standard regression bounds (O(1/sqrt(n)) generalization error), which at n=100-200 implies substantial uncertainty in the learned return model. (3) PGMORL has no finite-sample bound; convergence to the Pareto front is only guaranteed in the limit of infinite policy gradient steps with decaying step size. In practice, MORL training curves on small data are highly sensitive to random seed and hyperparameter choices, with no reliable convergence indicators.
reward_distribution_handling: MORL addresses reward distribution challenges differently per objective: (1) Hit-count objective (r1): inherits the sparsity problem of standard RL — ~95% of plays yield r1=0, causing Q1(s,a) estimates to concentrate near zero with high variance. Reward shaping (r1 = hits/k, range 0.0-1.0) helps; distributional extensions (IQN-style vector Q-function) can model the full return distribution per objective. (2) Diversity objective (r2): the coverage/diversity reward can be computed deterministically from the set of generated plays (average pairwise Hamming distance, entropy of number frequency), giving a dense, low-variance reward signal that stabilizes training even when r1 is sparse. This is a key advantage of MORL over single-objective RL: r2 provides a learning signal on every update even when r1=0. (3) Minimum draws needed for stable MORL: approximately 200-500 for simple PCN-style regression; 1000+ for policy-gradient MORL (PGMORL, Envelope DQN). (4) The two-objective formulation (hit-count + diversity) partially solves the sparsity problem because diversity reward is dense.
credit_assignment_granularity: MORL does not inherently change credit assignment granularity — it depends on the base algorithm. For the lottery application with MORL: (1) Hit-count objective (r1): best implemented with number-level (semi-bandit) credit — each number in a play that matches the actual draw contributes +1/k to r1, providing k independent learning signals per draw rather than one. This is straightforward to implement with play-level MORL. (2) Diversity objective (r2): naturally operates at play-batch level — r2 is computed across all plays in a ticket (e.g., 3 plays per ticket), measuring how well the set of plays covers different regions of the number space. This batch-level credit is unique to MORL and not available in single-objective RL without explicit diversity reward. (3) Combining both: PCN receives the vector reward [r1, r2] per ticket, allowing the network to learn both number-level hit patterns and batch-level diversity patterns from the same 100-200 historical draws.
diversity_mechanism: Diversity is a first-class objective in MORL rather than a regularization afterthought: (1) Explicit diversity reward (r2) — computed as the mean pairwise Hamming distance between plays in a ticket (e.g., 3 plays of k=7 numbers): higher distance = more diverse coverage. This makes diversity directly optimizable and measurable. (2) Pareto front diversity — by training over the full range of preference vectors w = [w1, w2] with w1 + w2 = 1, the PCN learns policies ranging from pure hit-maximization (w = [1, 0]) to pure diversity-maximization (w = [0, 1]), with all intermediate tradeoffs available at inference by selecting w. (3) Set-cover metric as r2 — alternatively, r2 can be defined as the fraction of the ball pool {1..N} covered by at least one play in the ticket, incentivizing plays to collectively cover different number regions. (4) Population-based diversity (PGMORL) — maintains multiple policies simultaneously, each optimized for a different Pareto weight, with explicit population diversity maintained via evolutionary selection. The explicit diversity objective eliminates the need for entropy coefficient tuning, which is a major practical advantage over single-objective methods.
offline_vs_online_rl_compatibility: MORL algorithms vary widely in offline compatibility: (1) PCN (best for lottery-nn) — can be trained fully offline as a supervised regression problem on historical draws; requires only a static dataset of (draw_history, preference_vector, achievable_returns) triples. Offline compatible with no environment interaction. (2) Envelope Q-learning — offline compatible with a replay buffer, analogous to offline DQN; requires careful handling of distributional shift when the behavior policy (historical plays) differs from the learned policy. (3) PGMORL — fundamentally online; requires iterative policy rollouts to evolve the population of Pareto-optimal policies. Not directly applicable to weekly draw cycle without extensive synthetic augmentation. (4) GPI-LS (Generalized Policy Improvement with Linear Scalarization) — can operate offline over a fixed set of policy evaluations, making it partially compatible. Verdict: PCN is the only MORL-Baselines algorithm that is straightforwardly applicable to the offline, fixed-dataset (100-200 draws) lottery setting. The combination of offline compatibility and preference conditioning makes PCN the recommended MORL approach for lottery-nn Phase 2.
key_dependencies: morl-baselines (pip install morl-baselines, https://github.com/LucasAlegre/morl-baselines), PyTorch (already present), numpy, gymnasium (for environment interface), scipy (for Pareto front computation and hypervolume indicator). PCN specifically requires only PyTorch and numpy — it is the lightest MORL-Baselines algorithm. Full MORL-Baselines install pulls in stable-baselines3 and wandb as optional dependencies.
estimated_lines_of_code: 400-600 lines of new code for PCN integration: preference-conditioned actor head (60 lines), vector critic with 2-objective Q-function (80 lines), diversity reward computation across plays (50 lines), Pareto front sampling and preference vector scheduler (80 lines), offline PCN training loop with historical draw replay (120 lines), multi-objective evaluation and hypervolume logging (80 lines), inference-time preference selection and play generation (60 lines). Excludes MORL-Baselines library code itself. Full PGMORL integration would require 800-1000 additional lines for population management.
transfer_learning_compatibility: High compatibility for PCN; medium for other MORL algorithms. The existing SharedLotteryTransformer encoder is ideal as the backbone: (1) PCN adds a preference vector concatenation layer before the actor head — the encoder output (embedding) is concatenated with the 2D preference vector w and passed to the actor and critic heads. Only the heads require new parameters; the pretrained encoder is reused intact. (2) The lottery_id embedding already handles per-lottery differentiation, so MORL per-lottery objective definitions (e.g., LottoMax has 7-number plays so diversity reward is defined differently from 5-number Daily Grand) are naturally handled. (3) The pretrained backbone provides a strong feature initialization that reduces the data needed for MORL regression training, which is critical at n < 200. (4) For PGMORL: the population of policies can all share the pretrained encoder backbone, with separate lightweight actor heads per policy, reducing total parameter count and training instability.
specific_application_in_project: MORL would be used in Phase 2 to solve the specific tension between two conflicting goals in lottery play generation: (1) maximizing expected hits (concentrate plays on highest-frequency number subsets) and (2) maximizing coverage (spread plays across underrepresented numbers to hedge against model uncertainty). Concrete implementation: (a) Define r1 = number of hits per play (0-7 for LottoMax), normalized to [0,1]. (b) Define r2 = mean pairwise Hamming distance across the 3 plays in a ticket (coverage metric), normalized to [0,1]. (c) Train a preference-conditioned PCN actor that takes [encoder_output | preference_vector_w] and generates plays whose expected (r1, r2) tradeoff matches w. (d) At inference time, expose a --coverage parameter (0.0=pure hit focus, 1.0=pure diversity) that sets w and generates tickets along the Pareto front. (e) Use MORL-Baselines GPI-LS to identify the knee point of the Pareto front (best single operating point balancing both objectives) as the default. This replaces the current temperature parameter in src/predict.py with a semantically meaningful coverage-vs-hits knob. All three lotteries share the encoder; per-lottery Pareto fronts differ only in head dimensions and play size. Phase 2 timeline: implement after basic Actor-Critic (REINFORCE-with-baseline) is working.
replaces_or_extends: Extends existing temperature-softmax sampling in src/predict.py — the MORL preference vector w replaces the single temperature parameter, decomposing the implicit diversity-vs-exploitation tradeoff into an explicit two-objective optimization. The SharedLotteryTransformer backbone is extended with a preference-conditioned actor head and a 2-objective critic head; the encoder itself is unchanged.
existing_open_source_implementations: 1. MORL-Baselines (https://github.com/LucasAlegre/morl-baselines) — official implementation by Felten et al. 2023, includes PCN, GPI-LS, Envelope Q-learning, PGMORL, CAPQL under a unified Gymnasium-compatible API; pip install morl-baselines; actively maintained as of 2025. 2. PCN reference implementation (https://github.com/mathieu-reymond/pareto-conditioned-networks) — Reymond & Nowe original PCN code, simpler but less integrated. 3. pymoo (https://pymoo.org) — not RL-specific but provides Pareto front computation utilities (NSGA-II, hypervolume indicator) used for evaluating MORL policies. 4. multi-objective-rl (https://github.com/RunzheYang/MORL) — Yang et al. 2019 Envelope Q-learning for MORL, PyTorch-based. 5. No lottery-specific MORL reference implementation exists; the combinatorial action adaptation (autoregressive masking for k-of-N) must be implemented from scratch on top of any of the above.
benchmark_results: MORL-Baselines (Felten et al. 2023) benchmarks: (1) MO-MuJoCo (continuous control, 2-4 objectives): PCN achieves 85-95% of the hypervolume of the true Pareto front on MO-HalfCheetah and MO-Hopper with 1M environment steps; GPI-LS outperforms PGMORL on most tasks. (2) Deep Sea Treasure (discrete action, sparse reward): PCN achieves near-optimal Pareto front coverage with 50K steps; Envelope Q-learning converges but is slower. (3) MO-Reacher (continuous, 2 objectives): GPI-LS achieves the highest hypervolume indicator (0.91 vs 0.78 for PGMORL). (4) All benchmarks use online interaction with 50K-1M environment steps — no small offline dataset benchmarks. (5) Pareto front quality (hypervolume indicator): PCN typically achieves 80-95% of optimal hypervolume on 2-objective tasks; degrades to 60-70% on 3-4 objectives. (6) No direct combinatorial discrete set-output benchmarks exist in the MORL-Baselines paper.
notable_use_cases: 1. Multi-objective recommendation systems — slate generation (select k items from N candidates) with competing objectives of relevance and diversity; structurally identical to lottery play generation (k-of-N, diversity vs. hit rate). Industrial recommendation at YouTube, Netflix uses MORL-style preference weighting to balance click-through rate vs. watch-time vs. content diversity. 2. Portfolio optimization — select k assets from N candidates to maximize expected return while minimizing variance; combinatorial structure with two competing objectives directly analogous to lottery coverage-vs-hits. 3. Drug discovery — select k molecular fragments from a pool to maximize binding affinity while maintaining structural diversity; sparse reward, combinatorial action space, small datasets (high structural similarity to lottery application). 4. Multi-objective combinatorial optimization (MOCO) — MORL applied to Traveling Salesman with time and distance objectives; autoregressive pointer networks with preference conditioning; same architecture pattern applicable to lottery play generation. 5. Clinical trial design — select k patients for treatment from N candidates, balancing efficacy (hit rate analog) and population coverage (diversity analog); small dataset regime (100-500 patients) with direct methodological parallels.
